title: Architecture & Standards: Unified API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, and Performance Guidelines
author: Jordan Reyes
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's cross-cutting architecture and engineering standards for: API design, coding conventions, infrastructure (IaC) patterns, model-serving best practices, observability, and performance targets. It is intended as the canonical reference for engineering teams implementing services and model deployments across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private products.

Goals
- Provide consistent, reviewable standards to reduce production incidents and improve developer velocity.
- Ensure predictable operational characteristics (latency, cost, availability).
- Establish clear ownership and decision records (ADRs) for significant architectural choices.

Scope and audience
- Scope: Service APIs, backend services, deployment IaC, model-serving components, telemetry pipelines, and performance SLOs.
- Audience: Service owners, backend engineers, infra engineers, model-onboarding owners, SRE, and security.

1) API Standards
Purpose: APIs are the public surface area that other engineers and customers rely on. Maintain backward compatibility, consistent error handling, and clear versioning.

Key rules
- Design-first approach: Use OpenAPI 3.1 schema for REST endpoints and Protobuf v3 for internal binary RPCs. Store canonical OpenAPI specs in the central api-specs repo (repo: infra/api-specs).
- Versioning: Use path-based major versions: /v1/, /v2/. Minor changes must be backward compatible. Remove deprecated endpoints only after a 90-day deprecation window and stakeholder communication.
- Idempotency: Write endpoints that mutate state must accept an idempotency-key header.
- Pagination: Use cursor-based pagination for list endpoints. Provide next_cursor in responses.
- Field naming: snake_case for JSON keys across services. Timestamps must be RFC3339 (UTC).
- Error model: Standardize on the following JSON error envelope: {"code": string, "message": string, "details": optional list}. Map HTTP codes: 400 (validation), 401 (auth), 403 (permission), 404 (not_found), 429 (rate_limited), 500 (server_error).
- Rate limiting: Responses must include X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset headers for public APIs.

API security
- All external endpoints must require mTLS or OAuth2 bearer (per product). Keys and tokens stored in KMS.
- Input validation: Reject payloads over configured max size. Default max request size: 2MB for non-streaming endpoints.

Examples and tooling
- Publish OpenAPI docs via the docs-site CI pipeline. Use swagger-cli for validation as part of PRs.
- Example: generation endpoint snippet in OpenAPI: |
  paths:
    /v1/generate:
      post:
        summary: Text generation

2) Coding Standards
Purpose: Maintain readable, secure, and testable code across services.

Language conventions
- Python: follow PEP8 + black formatter and isort. Minimum supported runtime: Python 3.10. Use typing (mypy) for public modules.
- Go: follow Effective Go; use gofmt and golangci-lint. Target Go 1.20+.
- Rust/CPP: reserved for performance-critical runtime components; follow team-specific style guides and use CI formatting.

CI and quality gates
- Pre-commit: Enforce linters, formatters, and simple static checks locally.
- PRs: Require at least one reviewer and successful CI including unit tests and security-scan. Merge only when status checks pass.
- Test coverage: Services must aim for 70%+ unit test coverage on critical path code. Integration tests required for infra and model-serving changes that affect production behavior.

Dependency and secrets management
- Lock dependencies (pipfile.lock/go.sum). Approve dependency upgrades via an automated dependabot flow and security review for any CVE severity >= HIGH.
- Secrets must never be committed. Use environment-backed KMS secrets or HashiCorp Vault.

3) Infrastructure & IaC Standards
Purpose: Define standard patterns for networking, IAM, cost allocation, and deployment artifacts.

IaC rules
- Terraform (v1.4+) is the canonical tooling for cloud infra. Modules stored in terraform-modules repo. Use a module-per-responsibility pattern.
- Naming: resources use the pattern rdx-{team}-{env}-{service}-{component} when possible.
- Tagging: All cloud resources must include tags: team, service, environment, cost_center, compliance.
- Environments: dev, staging, prod. Staging must mirror production region topology and at least 50% of capacity.

Networking and security
- VPCs: Use per-customer VPCs for Private deployments. Use VPC peering or transit gateway for platform components.
- Firewalls: Default deny inbound; allow only required service ports. Bastion access limited with session recording.
- KMS/HSM: All at-rest keys for customer data must be managed through KMS. Encryption in transit via TLS 1.2+ (prefer TLS1.3).

Deployment and release
- Immutable artifacts: Docker images with semantic version tags and digest pinned in deployment manifests.
- Blue/green or canary: Production deploys must have automated rollback criteria (see Rollout policy section below).

4) Model-Serving Standards
Purpose: Ensure model deployments are safe, cost-efficient, and observable.

Model lifecycle and registry
- Model registry: All production models must be registered in the model-registry (repo/service: model-registry). Metadata required: model_id, architecture, training_commit, quantization_profile, variant, owner, expected_token_cost.
- Versioning: Use semver-like scheme for model variants: <model>-v<major>.<minor>.<patch>-<quant>. Example: llama2-v1.3.0-4bit.
- Approval: Model onboarding requires a checklist: unit evals, safety evals, cost estimates, and a signed owner approval.

Serving configuration
- KV cache: Default per-model KV cache TTL = 24h for prefix caching. Provide explicit cache keys for prompt fingerprints.
- Quantization profiles: Store quant profiles per-model in quantization-profiles directory; use experiment-backed recommendations from Redwood Optimize.
- Fallbacks: Every critical model route must declare at least one compatible fallback variant in case of capacity/health issues.
- Autoscaling: Serve with target CPU/GPU utilization and queue-length based autoscalers. Default target GPU util: 70% (adjust per model workload).

Safety and privacy
- PII handling: Any model that stores or logs customer-provided prompts must redact PII before persisted logs. Use the data-management guidelines for retention.

Operational playbooks
- Model rollback: To rollback a bad model: 1) Trigger immediate traffic shift to fallback model; 2) Isolate problematic variant; 3) Create a postmortem if user-facing impact occurred.

5) Observability Standards
Purpose: Ensure teams can detect, triage, and resolve incidents quickly.

Telemetry primitives
- Traces: OpenTelemetry instrumentation for inter-service traces. All external request spans must include trace context and service= tags.
- Metrics: Use Prometheus client libraries and common metric name prefixes rdx_ (e.g., rdx_request_duration_seconds).
- Logs: Structured JSON logs with keys: timestamp, level, service, env, request_id, user_id (if applicable), message. Use logback or equivalent for Java/Python apps.

Dashboards and alerts
- Dashboards: Every service must publish a standard dashboard with: request rate, error rate, p95/p99 latency, queue length, GPU utilization (if applicable), and cost/s token burn.
- Alerting: Use PagerDuty for high-severity. Standard alert thresholds (examples):
  - High error rate: error_rate_5m > 0.5% for 5+ min -> SEV2
  - Latency SLO breach: p95 latency > target * 1.5 for 5+ min -> SEV2
  - GPU OOMs: any OOM spike -> SEV1
- On-call runbooks: Link runbooks in the dashboard. Include a contact list and escalation path.

Tracing and correlation
- Correlate logs and metrics using a single request_id and trace_id propagated end-to-end. Requests entering the platform must include x-request-id; if missing, generate at edge.

6) Performance Standards and SLOs
Purpose: Define measurable targets to achieve predictable customer experience while optimizing cost.

SLOs (examples; service owners may set stricter values)
- Availability: 99.9% (monthly uptime) for Hosted API generation endpoints (SLO target). Error budget: 43.2 minutes/month.
- Latency: P95 end-to-end latency targets (excluding streaming) for typical hosted text generation routes: small models p95 < 150ms, medium models p95 < 350ms, large/LLM p95 < 800ms.
- Throughput: Per-GPU token throughput baselines documented in benchmarking-and-perf-suite. Target utilization: 65-85% depending on customer SLAs.
- Cold start: Cold start SHOULD be < 2s for light-weight model variants and < 10s for large host loads. Track cold-starts and include in SLO reporting.

Cost and batching guidance
- Batching: Use adaptive batching with max effective batch size tuned per model. For interactive workloads, target median batch size <= 4; for high-throughput background workloads, batches 8-64.
- Caching: Use prefix/KV caching and result caching for repeated prompts. Expected cost savings and hit-rate documented per route.

7) Rollout and Release Policies (Cross-cutting)
- Canary: New model variants and service releases must go through canary traffic (default 2% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%), with automated health checks at each step.
- Automated rollback criteria: error_rate_increase > 50% baseline OR latency p95 > 2x baseline OR cost-per-token > budget_threshold -> automatic rollback.
- Human approval gating: Major changes (schema, API-breaking, cross-region infra) require product and security sign-off.

8) Decision Records and ADR Index
We track architectural decisions as lightweight ADRs (Architecture Decision Records) in the docs repo. Below are key recent ADRs and owners: 

| ADR ID | Title | Decision summary | Owner | Link |
|--------|-------|------------------|-------|------|
| ADR-2024-01 | Kernel selection strategy | Use hardware-aware kernel selection with runtime profiling and a fallback kernel for compatibility | Runtime team | /confluence/architecture-and-standards/adr-2024-01-kernel-selection |
| ADR-2024-07 | Quantization default policy | Default to 4-bit quantization profiles for cost-sensitive production variants with evaluation gates | Applied ML | /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/adr-2024-07-quantization |
| ADR-2025-03 | OpenAPI-first for public APIs | Adopt OpenAPI as the source of truth for public endpoints and auto-generate SDKs | Eng DX | /confluence/eng-developer-experience/adr-2025-03-openapi-first |
| ADR-2025-11 | Metrics naming and rdx_ prefix | Standardize metric names and adopt rdx_ prefix across services | Eng SRE | /confluence/eng-sre/adr-2025-11-metrics-naming |

9) Ownership and Governance
- Document owner: Architecture Guild (rotating leads). Day-to-day editorial: Architecture review board (ARB).
- Change process: Propose changes via ADR or PR against this document. Major changes require at least two reviewers from ARB and SRE.

10) Templates and Checklists (quick references)
- API review checklist (must be completed before public API merge): OpenAPI schema present, pagination defined, idempotency keys for mutates, auth defined, and integration tests pass.
- Model onboarding checklist: registry entry, safety evals, perf baseline, quant profile, fallback defined, owner approval.
- Infra PR checklist: Terraform plan reviewed, cost impact estimated, tags present, IAM principle of least privilege verified.

Appendix A: Example config snippets
- Example OpenAPI snippet:
  components:
    schemas:
      GenerateRequest:
        type: object
        properties:
          prompt:
            type: string
          max_tokens:
            type: integer
            default: 256

- Example Prometheus metric names:
  rdx_request_duration_seconds_bucket
  rdx_requests_total{status="500"}

Appendix B: How to propose an ADR
1) Create a short ADR document in docs/adr with: context, decision, consequences, alternatives considered.
2) Open PR and tag architecture-guild and affected teams.
3) After two approving reviews and one SRE sign-off, merge.

Contact and follow-up
- Architecture Guild Slack channel: #arch-guild.
- ARB rotation: see /confluence/architecture-and-standards/arb-rotations.
